clue.text: Wherewith the pupils give themselves airs?

definitions.text: Wherewith the pupils give themselves airs?

parts.words: Wherewith the pupils give themselves airs
parts.note: the pupils are those of the eyes, which wear spectacles; airs are tunes, played by rubbing wet rims of tumblers

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren putting on superior manners, and asking what helps them do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' suggests schoolchildren and 'give themselves airs' suggests snobbery; read instead as eye pupils behind spectacles, and airs as tunes played on a set of tuned tumblers.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of tuned drinking tumblers played as an instrument gives out tunes, while spectacles are what eye pupils look through.

clue.text: Is it churned out at the bar? .

definitions.text: Is it churned out at the bar?

parts.words: Is it churned out at the bar
parts.note: a milk bar serves a whisked dairy drink; 'churned' suggests butter-making and 'bar' a pub

explanation.surface: A question about what a pub produces in quantity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; here it is a milk bar, and 'churned' is the whisking that makes the drink frothy.
explanation.definitionFit: A frothy whisked drink of milk and flavouring is the staple served at a milk bar.

clue.text: It's the outside limit, says a skilled man on board

parts.note: riding a board over waves is to surf
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A surfer explains where the edge of things lies.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'skilled man on board' is a surf ace, an expert surfer, and what he 'says' is just those two words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: The outermost layer or boundary of a thing is its face or exterior.

clue.text: Such our society in a teachers strike

definitions.text: Such our society in a teachers strike

parts.words: Such our society in a teachers strike
parts.note: when teachers stop work the pupils are left without lessons; read socially, it describes a society without ranks

explanation.surface: A remark that a teachers' strike makes all of us equal.
explanation.walkthrough: The word splits as CLASS LESS: no lessons during a strike; but as one word it describes a society without social ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: A society with no social ranks is one where hierarchy has been abolished, just as a school strike leaves pupils without lessons.

clue.text: Harken to item after item

definitions.meaning: to hearken, or pay attention, is the archaic verb '...', as in Hamlet's '..., ..., O ...!'
a series of items written one below another is an inventory

explanation.surface: An instruction to pay attention to a recitation of items.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic verb meaning to pay attention, and a catalogue of items written one after another.

clue.text: See 1
How can they be detailed for experiments?

definitions.text: How can they be detailed for experiments?

parts.words: How can they be detailed for experiments
parts.note: 'detailed' reads as de-tailed, tails removed, and these rodents have no tails; laboratory animals are assigned to tests

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how lab animals get assigned to tests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' means assigned, but read as de-tailed it asks how a tailless animal could lose its tail. These rodents have no visible tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailless cavies are the classic laboratory test animals, so anyone used in a trial is called by their name.

clue.text: A latter day chap in the commercial world?

definitions.text: A latter day chap in the commercial world?

parts.words: A latter day chap in the commercial world
parts.note: AD (anno Domini) marks the latter era and a chap is a man; together they name an advertising man

explanation.surface: A question about a modern-day businessman.
explanation.walkthrough: AD, anno Domini, labels the later era of the calendar, and a chap is a MAN; together they make the advertising man of the commercial world.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who works in advertising is a creature of commerce and of the modern age.

clue.text: This dale is not in the Basque country

definitions.text: This dale is not in the Basque country

parts.words: This dale is not in the Basque country
parts.note: this word plus 'dale' gives the name of a Berkshire village with a golf course; 'Basque' sounds like bask, lying in the sun

explanation.surface: A geographical note that a certain valley lies outside the Basque region.
explanation.walkthrough: Sunningdale is a village in Berkshire, England, so 'this' plus 'dale' is not in the Basque country; yet the word itself means basking, which 'Basque' sounds like.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying out in the sun to warm oneself is basking, which is what 'Basque' sounds like.

clue.text: For writing a motto on a sundial ? And how!

definitions.text: For writing a motto on a sundial ? And how!

parts.words: For writing a motto on a sundial ? And how
parts.note: a stylus for writing, the pointer that casts a sundial's shadow, and a manner of doing things all share one name

explanation.surface: A question about how to engrave an inscription on a sundial.
explanation.walkthrough: Three senses: a pointed writing tool, the projecting pointer (gnomon) on a sundial, and manner, the 'how' of doing something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an ancient pointed writing tool, the shadow-casting pin on a sundial, and a characteristic manner.

clue.text: Right in the middle of molten rock there's grub

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, sitting in its centre

parts.note: lava is molten rock from a volcano

explanation.surface: Something edible found in the heart of a lava flow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle of' puts R (right) inside LAVA.
explanation.definitionFit: A grub is the soft wormlike young of an insect, its immature stage.

clue.text: What Charles I might have meant by the floating pound ?

definitions.text: What Charles I might have meant by the floating pound

parts.words: What Charles I might have meant by the floating pound
parts.note: a floating pound is a currency left to find its value; Charles I levied a tax to pay for the navy

explanation.surface: A quip that a Stuart king anticipated the floating exchange rate.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles I raised a much-resented tax, nominally for the navy, from inland counties too; money for floating vessels is a pun on the modern 'floating pound' currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The levy Charles I imposed to fund the fleet was a charge for seagoing vessels, so a 'pound' meant for things that float.

clue.text: Spares for repair in short supply

indicators.note: something sent for repair is taken apart and rebuilt, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Replacement parts for mending things are hard to come by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For repair' rearranges SPARES.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarce and thinly spread things are few and far between.

clue.text: While waiting on the clock ?

definitions.meaning: in the interval between events, meanwhile
Greenwich ... is the average solar time shown on clocks

explanation.surface: Watching the clock while waiting for something.
explanation.definitionFit: The interval meanwhile, and the averaged solar reckoning that clocks keep, as at Greenwich.

clue.text: Wild life recently seen here in a 27

definitions.text: Wild life recently seen here in a 27

parts.words: Wild life recently seen here in a 27
parts.note: the wild life is a South African antelope, and the touring South African rugby side shares its name, seen pushing in a scrum (27)

explanation.surface: A naturalist's note on animals recently spotted locally.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 is SCRUM. The antelope gives its name to South Africa's rugby team, which had recently toured Britain, so it was seen packing down in scrums.
explanation.definitionFit: South African antelopes give their name to the national rugby team, whose forwards pack down in scrums.

clue.text: Poplar victim, East End

parts.note: Abel, killed by Cain, was the Bible's first murder victim
E is the abbreviation for East; London's East End is home to the district of Poplar

explanation.surface: A crime victim in Poplar, a district of London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: Poplar is a district in London's East End, so the surface reads as a local crime report; here it is the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The white poplar is a tree also known by an old name from Dutch.

clue.text: Entertainer at an Eton "social"?

parts.note: Pop is the elite society of senior boys at Eton College, so a vocalist at its social is a singer at Pop

explanation.surface: A performer booked for a school party at Eton.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop is the self-electing society of senior boys at Eton College, the English public school; a singer at its social would be a singer of Pop.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer of chart music, read here as someone singing for the Eton society called Pop.

clue.text: I am over-busy to be much affected

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
someone hard pressed has too much to do

explanation.surface: Someone says they are too busy to be deeply moved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I am over-busy' reads as I'M PRESSED, which run together means strongly moved.
explanation.definitionFit: To be deeply moved or struck by something is to be made a strong mark on.

clue.text: Milko ! Canon does he sing?

definitions.meaning: the milkman's cry as he makes his delivery circuit
a canon is a round, a song with staggered entries, so a singer of them

explanation.surface: A milkman calling out on his rounds, and whether he sings in church.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman doing a daily delivery circuit, like the milkman, and one who sings canons, which are rounds.

clue.text: Back me giving orders for raising figures outstandingly

indicators.note: 'back' tells us to read the word me in the other direction

parts.note: to boss is to give orders

explanation.surface: Support me while I give orders to lift people outstandingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reverses ME to give EM, followed by BOSSING. 'Outstandingly' means standing out from the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamping designs so that they stand proud of the surface is relief work on metal or paper.

clue.text: Oval rib operated on for Simon

indicators.note: a surgeon operating cuts and rearranges, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone called Simon has had surgery on an oval rib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operated on' rearranges OVAL RIB. Simon Bolivar was the South American liberator.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Bolivar was the liberator of much of South America, so the first name points to the surname.

clue.text: Frank military man

parts.note: a Frank is a Frenchman, so this is a French soldier, the nickname from the First World War

explanation.surface: An honest, outspoken soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like an adjective for candid; read as a Frenchman, it asks for the hairy French infantryman of the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: French infantrymen of the First World War were nicknamed 'hairy ones', and a Frank is a Frenchman.

clue.text: Collects in a camp between north and south

parts.note: inter is the Latin for between, as in interval

explanation.surface: Someone gathers people in a camp lying between north and south.
explanation.walkthrough: INTER, from the Latin prefix meaning between, is followed by N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding enemy aliens or prisoners together in a camp is confining them there in wartime.

clue.text: Barking University types

parts.note: at Oxford and Cambridge, the proctors' attendants have a dog's nickname, and dogs bark

explanation.surface: Students at a university in Barking, a district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of east London, so the surface suggests a local college; the types are the Oxford and Cambridge proctors' attendants, nicknamed after a dog breed, and dogs bark.
explanation.definitionFit: The proctors' attendants at Oxford and Cambridge carry the name of a stocky dog breed, one that barks.

clue.text: The second Mrs. Gargery

parts.note: in Dickens's Great Expectations, Joe Gargery remarries after his first wife dies, choosing the village schoolteacher

explanation.surface: A question about Joe Gargery's second wife.
explanation.walkthrough: In Great Expectations, Joe the blacksmith marries the kind village teacher after his harsh first wife dies.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Joe the blacksmith takes Pip's friend, the kind young village teacher, as his second wife.

clue.text: "The plaintive numbers "

parts.note: Wordsworth's The Solitary Reaper asks 'Will no one tell me what she sings? Perhaps the plaintive numbers flow'; numbers here are verses

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth about a sad song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' means verses or songs, not figures; the phrase comes from Wordsworth's The Solitary Reaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A mournful song or lament is plaintive verse, and 'numbers' is the poetic word for verses.

clue.text: Sailor Edward in session

parts.note: the sea is the sailor's domain, standing in for him here, as in 'gone to sea'
Ted is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A sailor named Edward attends a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: TED is the usual short form of Edward. The SEA for 'sailor' is loose: the setter lets the sailor's element stand for him.
explanation.definitionFit: A court or meeting in session is sitting, with its members in their places.

clue.text: A period expression

definitions.meaning: a fixed span of time, such as a school or court session
a word or phrase, as in 'a technical word'

explanation.surface: A phrase that describes a stretch of history.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a span of time, as in an academic session, and a word or phrase.

clue.text: Swimmer in straits

parts.note: a flatfish named after the channel port is caught in the Strait of Dover; 'in straits' also suggests trouble

explanation.surface: A cross-Channel swimmer in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' suggests a Channel swimmer and 'in straits' trouble; it is a fish named after the English port on the Strait of Dover.
explanation.definitionFit: A prized flatfish takes its name from the port on the narrow channel between England and France.

clue.text: Pushing forwards

parts.note: in rugby the forwards bind together and shove against the other pack

explanation.surface: Pressing ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forwards' looks like an adverb; it is the noun, the rugby forwards, who shove against each other in this set piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The rugby set piece in which the two packs of forwards bind and shove against each other.

clue.text: Nearly full pitchers

parts.note: jugs that are almost full; in cricket a full-pitched ball lands at the batsman's feet

explanation.surface: Jugs filled almost to the brim.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a full toss reaches the batsman without bouncing; a ball pitched just short of that lands at the batsman's feet, under the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket deliveries pitched right up at the batsman's toes, almost full tosses.

clue.text: Is mad on wandering in the Avenue

indicators.note: wandering letters stray from their places, so these are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone is mad on strolling along the avenue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' rearranges IS MAD ON. Madison Avenue in New York is the home of American advertising.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York thoroughfare famous for advertising agencies is named after President Madison.
